    1         I.       INTRODUCTION

    2    Q.         PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

    3    A.         My name is David E. Dismukes. My business address is 5800 One Perkins Place Drive,

    4    Suite 5-F, Baton Rouge, Louisiana, 70808.

    5    Q.         HAVE YOU PREVIOUSLY FILED TESTIMONY IN THIS PROCEEDING?

    6    A.         Yes. I filed testimony in this proceeding on September 18, 2026, on behalf of The

    7    Petroleum Alliance of Oklahoma (“The Petroleum Alliance”).

    8    Q.         WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY?

    9    A.         The purpose of my rebuttal testimony is to respond to certain elements of the responsive

   10    testimony prepared by the Public Utility Division (“PUD”) of the Oklahoma Corporation

   11    Commission (“the Commission” or “OCC”) regarding the Extra-Large Power and Light (“XLPL”)

   12    tariff proposed by Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company (“OG&E” or “the Company”).


   13         II.      RESPONSE TO THE PUD

   14    Q.         PLEASE SUMMARIZE THE PUD’S POSITION REGARDING OG&E’S

   15    PROPOSED QUALIFICATION STANDARDS FOR THE XLPL TARIFF.

   16    A.         The PUD recommends that an appeals process be created for customers classified as

   17    “Customer Type 3.” Note that those customers falling under the “Customer Type 3” designation

   18    are those that have been identified as existing (not new) customers that may not be adding load but

   19    have new capacity requirements for other reasons such as the findings of third parties such as the

   20    Southwest Power Pool (“SPP”). The PUD recommends that OG&E give written notice to these

   21    customers, and the PUD Director, identifying the change in service conditions relied upon and the




                                                           2
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 58 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 4 OF 7




    1    additional accredited capacity that must be added. The PUD also recommends that existing

    2    customers found to fall into this classification be given thirty days to contest OGE’s finding.1

    3    Q.      WHAT IS THE BASIS FOR THIS RECOMMENDATION?

    4    A.      The PUD supports this recommendation by expressing concern that an existing customer

    5    can be forced to take service under the XLPL tariff based on the actions of other parties like the

    6    SPP. An example of how such a situation may arise could include a change in SPP reserve margin

    7    levels or calculations, resulting in an additional 75 MW or more of capacity being needed to serve

    8    an existing large load customer. The PUD's proposed notice and appeal process is intended to give

    9    these “Class 3” customers a meaningful opportunity to challenge that determination.

   10    Q.      DO YOU AGREE WITH THE PUD’S ALTERNATIVE RECOMMENDATION

   11    FOR THE XLPL TARIFF QUALIFICATION STANDARDS?

   12    A.      No since the proposal misses the fundamental problem with OGE’s classification which is

   13    that the classification is entirely inconsistent with the stated purpose of HB 2992, which makes

   14    clear that the legislature intended this tariff to target "new data centers, new cryptocurrency mining

   15    operations and new facilities whose primary function is artificial-intelligence computing

   16    facilities,"2 not existing customers reclassified due to circumstances outside their control.

   17    Moreover, these qualification standards are inconsistent with other electric utility service

   18    territories nationwide (see Exhibit DED-1 attached to my responsive testimony in this proceeding)

   19    as well as the PSO settlement tariff approved by the ALJ which limits large load classification to

   20    new and incremental capacity additions. 3 While the PUD recommendation is well intentioned, it

    1    is not needed since the Class 3 classification should be rejected out of hand as inconsistent with

    2    state public policy: in no way should this classification be “fixed.”

    3    Q.      PLEASE SUMMARIZE THE PUD’S POSITION REGARDING THE COMPANY’S

    4    PROPOSED CUSTOMER AFFORDABILITY CHARGE.

    5    A.      The PUD recommends that all revenue credits generated by this charge be allocated to all

    6    residential customers instead of being used to fund the Low-Income Assistance Program, Senior

    7    Citizen Discount credits, and energy efficiency and demand reduction programs. 4

    8    Q.      DO YOU AGREE WITH THE PUD’S ALTERNATIVE RECOMMENDATION

    9    RELATED TO THE CUSTOMER AFFORDABILITY CHARGE?

   10    A.      No. The PUD’s alternative proposals fails to address the fundamental problem with the

   11    Customer Affordability Charge, which is that the charge itself is not based on cost causation.

   12    OG&E argues that the Customer Affordability Charge is “cost-based” because its $2.50 per kW

   13    rate was designed to generate $30 million in revenues to offset the costs of funding the Low Income

   14    Assistance Program, an expansion of the Senior Citizen Discount to all seniors, and 20 percent of

   15    its residential energy efficiency and demand reduction program. 5 The Company’s assertion that

   16    the proposed Customer Affordability Charge is “cost-based” is inconsistent with how that term is

   17    used in utility regulation. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) defines “Cost-

   18    Based Rates” as “[a] ratemaking concept used for the design and development of rate schedules to

   19    ensure that the filed rate schedules recover only the cost of providing the service.”6 In contrast,

   20    the proposed Customer Affordability Charge is precisely the opposite of a cost-based rate because,

   21    instead of recovering the costs of providing service to XLPL customers, its purpose is to fund

    1    programs that overwhelmingly serve non-XLPL customers. This charge is simply a mechanism

    2    that arbitrarily transfers funds from XLPL customers to non-XLPL customers without any cost

    3    basis.


    4         III.         CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

    5    Q.          HAVE YOUR RECOMMENDATIONS CHANGED SINCE FILING RESPONSIVE

    6    TESTIMONY ON SEPTEMBER 18, 2026?

    7    A.          No.     Having reviewed the responsive testimony of intervening parties filed in this

    8    proceeding, I continue to recommend the Commission approve the proposed XLPL tariff with the

    9    following modifications:

   10                •     the proposed “Customer Type 3” qualification standard (and PUD’s proposed
   11                      modification) should be rejected and the qualification threshold limited to new
   12                      customer load and incremental load from existing customers equal to 75 MW or more;
   13                •     the proposed minimum billing demand equal to 85 percent of contract capacity should
   14                      be reduced to 80 percent;
   15                •     the collateral requirement should be reduced from 60 to 24 months of minimum bills;
   16                •     the Customer Class Protection Charge should be rejected, and instead, replaced by a
   17                      new charge modeled off the System Impact Charge recommended for approval by the
   18                      ALJ in the 2025 PSO base rate case (Case No. PUD 2025-000075);7
   19                •     the Customer Affordability Charge and Reservation Charge (as well as PUD’s
   20                      proposed change) should be rejected;
   21                •     OG&E should include an ongoing obligation to review any assets built to meet the
   22                      capacity needs of XLPL customers, including the potential for liquidation should one
   23                      or more XLPL service agreements end for any reason, with the XLPL customer class,
   24                      and not other ratepayers, bearing the costs of any shortfall if liquidation does not fully
   25                      recover an assets’ remaining book value; and
